title: ‘Mick Jagger should fold up his penis and go home’: the caustic genius of music critic Robert Christgau
text:
Rows and rows of CDs, albums, cassettes and books creak and groan on shelves that snake around the walls and choke the halls of an apartment in New York City’s East Village. The clutter that sprawls through its rooms is so dense it suggests the twistiest parts of a Moroccan medina or a warren no self-respecting rabbit would allow. Buried amid the muddle is a man hunched over a computer keyboard, clacking out words meant to make sense of all the sounds that this physical media holds.
Welcome to the lair of Robert Christgau, the self-declared “Dean of American Rock Critics”, as seen in a new documentary provocatively titled The Last Critic. “Bob is someone who has probably listened to more music, and published more words about music, than anyone to walk the face of the earth, and he’s still doing it in his mid-80s,” says Matty Wishnow, who directed the film. “It’s a career that’s both unprecedented and unrepeatable.”
It’s also one Christgau greatly advanced by creating a brand nearly 60 years ago called The Consumer Guide, a monthly feature for which he assigns albums letter grades that he weighs with the seriousness, and self-regard, of a judge at the Olympics. The ratings range from A+ (a score given to the New York Dolls’ thrilling, primitivist debut) to E, a category Christgau has written is “frequently cited as proof that there is no God”. (Guns N’ Roses’ 1988 GNR Lies is one unfortunate recipient of that distinction). As one of history’s first serious-minded rock critics, Christgau birthed his brand at the Village Voice, where he served, with rare breaks, as its chief music critic and editor from the late 1960s through 2006. After being fired by new management, he moved the column to a succession of other publications. Currently, it lives on Substack, which, his associates say, is one of the few such newsletters that generates a decent wage.
Wishnow says he was inspired to make the documentary by the formative influence Christgau had on his taste growing up. “I would open his collections of Consumer Guides and wonder: ‘Why is Queen a C- and Billy Joel a B- while this group called The Roches is an A+?’ It scrambled my brain and made me think of the idea of commercial versus credible and popular versus sub-popular,” he says. “When people ask me why I’m not into Yes or James Taylor, I think 30% of my answer is personal and 70% is something Bob wrote that imprinted itself on me.”
When he approached Christgau about making the film, Wishnow says it was hard at first to get him to commit the time. “Anything that takes Bob away from listening or writing or editing, his initial reaction is to bristle,” Wishnow says. “He’s visibly more comfortable listening than when the music is off.”
That helps explain why he hasn’t done interviews to promote the film, though the director said his subject is flattered and moved by it. The way Wishnow brought Christgau around reveals a crucial part of the critic’s character and also functions as the film’s heart. Key parts of the doc focus on Christgau’s relationship with his wife, Carola Dibbell, a critic, novelist and editor whom the director refers to as Bob’s esthetic partner. “She’s like a supplemental brain and response machine. On some level, the Consumer Guide represents Bob’s love letters to Carola.”
The two met in the late 1960s through a mutual friend in the East Village. Dibbell had been up all night doing mescaline, and within minutes, the two got into an argument about Jean-Luc Godard’s 1968 movie with the Rolling Stones, Sympathy for the Devil. In the doc, Dibbell says she immediately recognized that “this is the guy one has arguments with.”
As an aspiring journalist raised in Queens, New York, Christgau didn’t set out to become a critic. He wanted to be a sportswriter and his first story that got attention was on another subject entirely: a young woman who died on a macrobiotic diet. Not only did the piece win awards, but it also became a hallmark of the emerging “new journalism”. That success led to a column for Christgau at Esquire called Secular Music, which was wry code for “rock”, a form few over the age of 30 took seriously at the time. In 1969, when he started the Consumer Guide, the name was a kind of tease. “The idea of consumption was very far out of favor within bohemian culture,” Wishnow says. “Bob was challenging that idea, but he was also demonstrating his awareness that the music industry was both high art and big business.”
The idea of using a grading system for the Guide seemed equally off-putting to his youthful readers. Christgau responded to that in the film with, “If they can put a price on it, I can put a grade on it.”
The idea of calling himself “the dean of American rock critics” started as a drunken joke at a party after someone asked him who he was. The term stuck because of the clarity and authority of his opinions, as well as his aloof demeanor and merciless candor. In the film, a bevy of critics who’ve been edited by Christgau attest to the latter. “He’s blunt as fuck,” the late critic Greg Tate says on screen. “He’ll make you feel like the dumbest person in the world – but you will live,” reports Tricia Romano, the author of an oral history about the Village Voice, in the film.
Having been edited by Christgau myself decades ago, I can concur that the process can feel like a cross between a reality show elimination sequence and a frat house hazing. At the same time, the critics in the film, as well as yours truly, regard Christgau as one of the most generous and attentive editors a writer could hope for. He earned that reputation by cleanly separating his opinions from the writer’s. “As an editor, he was very clear that his job was to help the writer find the best version of their voice,” Wishnow says. “Even [the famed critic] Lester Bangs acknowledged that Bob was a great editor. And Lester was famously un-editable!”
Some of the artists Christgau has written most harshly about retain a certain respect for him as well. In the 1980s, Sonic Youth’s Thurston Moore was so frustrated by his coverage that he wrote a song called I Killed Christgau with My Big Fucking Dick. Even so, Wishnow says, “Thurston can blind recite some of Bob’s reviews. He’s a frenemy of Bob’s because they’re both New Yorkers and intellectuals. There’s a strange kind of warmth there.”
Far chillier was the response from Lou Reed. On his 1978 live album Take No Prisoners, Reed ranted, “can you imagine working for a fucking year and you got a B+ from some asshole in the Village Voice?” before going on to inquire, “what does Robert Christgau do in bed? Is he a toe-fucker?”
Christgau gave that album a C+ while thanking Lou “for pronouncing my name right”. Wishnow believes Christgau is privately flattered by the attention, though he has tried to keep a distance from the celebrities he covers to maintain his objectivity. Even so, some of his harshest reviews can feel awfully personal or can even cross a line. When reviewing Cass Elliott’s 1973 solo album Don’t Call Me Mama Anymore, he riffed on the title with a school-yard taunt, “How about Fatso?” “The line wasn’t funny then, and it’s not funny now,” Wishnow says. “But I would say that 99% of Bob’s negative reviews are simply strongly felt. It’s more of a ‘you-can-do-better’ attitude.”
Context also matters. Critics from the 1960s through the internet age were often read as much for their entertainment value and their bracing honesty as their erudition. And the audience generally accepted, and even enjoyed, a certain element of blood sport in the endeavor. Christgau used to exemplify that each November with his famous “Turkey Shoot” takedowns. But he stopped publishing negative reviews in 2005 because the task of listening repeatedly to albums he hated “became too taxing on him”, Wishnow says. “Today Bob’s negative biases are present by omission. If he doesn’t review it, you can assume he doesn’t like it.”
Friends of Christgau’s say that, over the years, he has mellowed some, aided by his role, along with Dibbell’s, as adoptive parents of their daughter Nina, who’s now 41. More, Nina opened him up to music he might have dismissed before, including Queen, whose T-shirt she sports in the film. Regardless, certain genres continue to irk and elude him, including prog rock, which he considers a “stupid” attempt to marry older notions of European music to rock, and heavy metal, which he barely considers at all. Of Black Sabbath’s world-changing 1970 debut, he wrote “the worst of the counterculture on a plastic platter. I’ve been worried something like this was going to happen ever since the first time I saw a numerology column in an underground newspaper.”
If pans like that sear into the reader’s consciousness, his raves have proven just as memorable. In an A assessment of Prince’s Dirty Mind in 1980, he noted the star’s sexual, as well as artistic, potency with the deathless kicker: “Mick Jagger should fold up his penis and go home.”
But it would be missing the point to focus too hard on Christgau’s individual lines. To Wishnow, the whole construction and concision of his capsule reviews is a surer mark of his genius. “Though he can’t go into depth because of the space constraints of the Guide, his reviews pack in elements of new journalism, politics and semiotics while also responding actively to the sound of the music – all in 150 words,” Wishnow says.
He calls that approach “intellectually athletic. A third of Bob’s sentences you don’t understand,” he says. “There are words you don’t know but, sometimes, he’ll write a sentence that is as good a sentence as has ever been written.”
Wishnow admits that the results can make for a dense read. Years ago, a reader sent a letter to the Voice accusing him of exactly that. “Madam”, Christgau responded in print, “my writing is no less dense than reality.” As the film shows, the reality of his own professional life cannot be separated from his personal relationship with his wife. He has even made it part of the public conversation, having written graphically about the couple’s sex life and having sported a T-shirt advocating for the power of monogamy, which is hardly a common rallying point in the bohemian world he inhabits.
In a true coup, the film features an interview with Randy Newman who reveals that he wrote his song Lost Without You about the couple’s relationship, something previously unknown to either the director or to Christgau. Wishnow compares the dichotomy of his character to a sour candy. “Once you get through the tartness of some of Bob’s ideas and, specifically, his sharp elbows and sharper language, you realize the inner part is unbelievably sweet,” he says.
At the same time, it reveals someone who’s unbelievably dedicated. At 84, he continues to crank out reams of reviews and Wishnow believes he’ll do so as long as he’s physically able, instigating a change with broader meaning. “When Bob stops doing this, it will be the end of something larger than just the Consumer Guide,” he says. “In my mind it will mark the end of a vocation.
“You could argue that today there are more music critics than ever, on X and Instagram and TikTok,” he allows. “But very few of them get paid for their work. Bob’s career as a professional critic represents the beginning, middle and end of something. He really is one of one.”
- The Last Critic is playing at Doc NYC, with a wider release to be announced
